newsitem.title: UK: BP offers to suspend damages claim vs Greenpeace.
newsitem.headline: BP offers to suspend damages claim vs Greenpeace.

text.p: British Petroleum on Tuesday offered to suspend a damages claim against Greenpeace if the environmental group agreed not to hinder its oil exploration and production in the north Atlantic any further.
BP had earlier launched a lawsuit against Greenpeace claiming 1.23 million pounds ($2 million) in damages for disruption to its operations after an eight-day protest by the environmentalists.
The company had also won a court injunction banning Greenpeace from disrupting its search for oil in the Foinaven field in the north Atlantic.
Greenpeace said it would abide by the court ruling but would not stop its campaign against the development of oil resources in the Atlantic frontier.
The interim interdict was granted by Edinburgh's Court of Session -- Scotland's highest civil court -- following a protest by Greenpeace members who boarded the Stena Dee floating oil platform.
The platform was headed from Norway to the Foinaven field some 100 miles off the coast of Scotland.
Greenpeace on Sunday called off the protest, saying it could no longer guarantee the activists' safety.
The environmental group said the legal action could bankrupt its operations in Britain, and appealed for public support in its court battle against BP.

"BP made 1.5 billion pounds profit in the first six months of the year -- it makes more in profit in 48 hours than Greenpeace receives in income in a year," Greenpeace deputy executive director Chris Rose said.
The four protesters who carried out the action on the Stena Dee were each fined 200 pounds in a Scottish court on Monday after pleading guilty to breaching the peace.

But the oil giant said in a statement: "BP's principal concern is not the recovery of damages. Rather, it is to ensure that its lawful operations are not interfered with and that safety is not compromised."

Greenpeace campaigners have also been blocking an Atlantic Richfield Co rig off the Alaskan coast to keep it away from a field in the Arctic Beaufort Sea. But a U.S. federal judge on Friday ordered them to stay outside a moving safety buffer around the mobile rig.
The blockades, aimed at fighting global warming, are part of Greenpeace's most ambitious campaign yet against the oil industry.
The group wants oil producers to switch to renewable resources, arguing that burning even existing reserves of fossil fuels will cause irreversible climate change.
